about.p: This book teaches the general vocabulary of academic English: the words you need in lectures, seminars, textbooks and essays whatever subject you study (*concept*, *put forward a theory*, *come to a conclusion*). It is especially useful for IELTS and for studying at an English-speaking university.

Each unit has a **left-hand page** that presents the vocabulary in short academic texts, tables and examples, and a **right-hand page** of exercises. The book stresses *word combinations* (which verbs, adjectives and prepositions go with a word) and *register* (which words are too formal for speech or too informal for writing).

about.-: Start with the units on key nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs, then study the combinations: academic vocabulary is learnt best in chunks such as *conduct research* or *a key factor*.

**Today** gives you new words and phrases every day and reviews them over time. **Units** has the left-hand page and the practice for each unit. *Over to you* asks you to write about your own subject.
The *Reading and vocabulary* units give you short academic texts with questions. The *Reference* section has formal and informal words, numbers and symbols, and British and American differences.

about.tip: Keep a record of words with their combinations, not single words: write *carry out an experiment*, not just *experiment*.

L.h: A Everyday words with academic meanings

L.p: Many academic words are ordinary words with a more specialised meaning. *Discipline* in a school is about behaviour; in academic English it is *an area of study*: Nanotechnology is a relatively new discipline.
Academic writing uses neutral and formal words. Informal words are fine in a seminar, but not in an essay.

Academic English often packs information into noun phrases. Instead of *Radiation was accidentally released and damaged a wide area*, a writer may say: *The accidental release of radiation caused widespread damage.* So learn the word family: accident, accidental, accidentally.

L.tip: Packing information into a noun phrase (*the long-term effects of widespread drought*) makes academic writing more concise, and examiners usually value it.

L.p: Academic style often uses a verb + a noun instead of a single verb: *explain* → *provide an explanation for*; *emphasise* → *place emphasis on*; *prove* → *offer proof that*.

text: Top athletes need good genes and good training, but they also need the right fuel. Optimal nutrition can make the difference between winning and losing, and misinformation about diet can do real harm.

The body's most valuable fuel during exercise is carbohydrate. In the early stages of moderate exercise, carbohydrates supply roughly half of the energy the body needs, and they yield more energy than fats for each unit of oxygen consumed. Because oxygen is often the limiting factor in long events, it makes sense for athletes to rely on the fuel that uses the least oxygen.

During digestion, carbohydrates are broken down into glucose, which is stored in the muscles and liver as glycogen. When we exercise, glycogen is converted back into glucose and used for energy. The ability to sustain prolonged, vigorous exercise is therefore closely related to the amount of glycogen stored before the event.

For events lasting less than about 90 minutes, normal glycogen stores are sufficient. For longer events, however, many endurance athletes eat a diet that is high in carbohydrate for two or three days beforehand, so that their glycogen stores are completely full at the start.

text: Until quite recently, many scientists held the view that our Solar System might be unique. Today, however, astronomers have detected planets orbiting thousands of other stars in our galaxy, and there is little reason to suppose that ours is the only system where life has evolved.

The Solar System comprises a central star, the Sun, and a large number of smaller, denser bodies: eight planets, their moons, dwarf planets, asteroids and comets. Most of these orbit the Sun in roughly the same plane, and the whole system moves around the centre of the Milky Way.

Stars are composed mainly of hydrogen and helium and are massive enough to sustain nuclear fusion, so they emit huge amounts of radiation. Planets, by contrast, are relatively cool and small. Some are rocky, like Earth and Mars; others, the giant planets, consist predominantly of gases and ices.

Pluto was regarded as the ninth planet from its discovery in 1930. However, astronomers later found thousands of similar icy objects beyond Neptune, in a region called the Kuiper Belt. As a consequence, in 2006 Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet.

text: In linguistics, *graphology* is the study of a language's writing system: the symbols used to write it, how many there are, and the rules for combining them. It must be distinguished from the popular sense of the word, the study of handwriting as a guide to personality, which most scientists regard as unreliable.

Linguistic graphology is an abstract study, just as phonology is the abstract study of a language's sound system. It is concerned not with the shape of a particular person's letters but with the units of the system itself, called *graphemes*, and how they interrelate.

Writing systems vary considerably. In an alphabetic system such as English, symbols broadly correspond to sounds, although the correspondence is often inconsistent. In a logographic system such as Chinese, symbols represent words or parts of words, while syllabic systems, such as Japanese kana, use one symbol for each syllable.
Understanding these differences helps to explain why learners from different backgrounds find different aspects of English spelling difficult.

text: Archaeological evidence suggests that early civilisations such as the Babylonians and Egyptians began to measure time at least 5,000 years ago. Calendars allowed them to coordinate public events, schedule trade and, above all, regulate the cycles of planting and harvesting.

These calendars were based on three natural cycles: the solar day, marked by the alternation of light and darkness as the earth rotates; the lunar month, which follows the phases of the moon; and the solar year, defined by the changing seasons as the earth revolves around the sun.

The problem was that these cycles do not fit neatly together. A solar year lasts about 365.25 days, which is not a whole number of lunar months. Successive calendars therefore introduced adjustments, such as extra months or leap years, to keep the calendar in line with the seasons.
Today, atomic clocks measure time with extraordinary precision, but the basic units we use, the day, the month and the year, still derive from these ancient observations.

text: Not everything people do is recorded in writing. Written and spoken records tend to be generated for unusual and important events, while the routine activities of daily life often go unrecorded. Nonetheless, written texts remain the basis on which most history is investigated.

Archaeological remains offer a way to access these unrecorded, mundane activities. Objects such as surgical instruments, pots for medicines and the design of buildings can reveal a great deal about how people looked after their health and how they understood illness.

This approach is particularly valuable for the study of medicine in the ancient world. Texts written by famous doctors tell us what educated men believed; artefacts can tell us what ordinary people actually did. By combining the two kinds of evidence, historians can build a fuller and more reliable picture of the past.

text: Visual images surround us as we work, play and learn. A typical classroom is full of pictures, diagrams, maps and graphs, and interactive whiteboards now allow teachers to project animations and annotate them as they talk. Textbooks are no longer predominantly made of text, and their digital versions are rich with video.

Technology has also changed how we create visualisations. Graphs no longer need to be plotted by hand from a table of values: anyone can draw them with software and even move part of a line to see how the equation changes.

Researchers argue that visualisation is not simply decoration. A well-designed diagram can reduce the load on working memory and help learners to see patterns that are hard to notice in words alone. A poorly designed one, however, may confuse rather than clarify. Learning to read and to create visual information is therefore becoming an essential academic skill.
